=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves are attached at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides, visible in multiple images)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): distal (leaves are spaced along the stem with noticeable gaps between nodes, not clustered)
B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): compound (each leaf is composed of multiple leaflets attached to a central rachis)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): odd-pinnate (leaflets arranged in pairs along a central axis with a single terminal leaflet, visible in close-up images)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): 7 (based on visible leaflets in the most complete compound leaf; 3 pairs plus one terminal leaflet)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): alternate (leaflets are arranged alternately along the rachis, not in pairs at the same node)
C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth without teeth or lobes, visible in close-up images)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): elliptic (leaflets are broadly oval with tapering ends, consistent across images)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tip of leaflets is sharply pointed, visible in multiple images)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): rounded (base of leaflets is broadly rounded, not tapered or heart-shaped)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (primary vein runs from base to apex, with secondary veins branching off to the sides, visible in close-up)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, spaced moderately, numerous (secondary veins clearly visible and running parallel to each other, spaced evenly)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (surface appears glossy and reflective, especially with water droplets)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs on leaf surface, surface appears smooth)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petiole is short relative to leaflet size, attaching leaflets close to rachis)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petiole is round in cross-section, no wings or grooves observed)
D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): herbaceous (stem is green, flexible, and lacks woody texture, typical of young seedlings)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs on stem surface)
    19. Stem color: green (stem is uniformly green, consistent across images)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (surface is smooth without ridges or lenticels)
E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules visible at leaf bases)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no latex exudate seen upon damage or breakage)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no swollen joints at leaflet bases visible; note: pulvinus is not clearly visible, but not observed)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): absent (no tendrils observed)
F. Notes: Some leaves show holes and margin damage, likely from herbivory, but cause not inferred. Seedling appears young, with multiple compound leaves. Pink tag visible, likely for field identification. All images show the same individual from different angles. Leaflet count based on most complete leaf; some leaflets partially obscured. No flowers or fruits visible.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Locating an individual
Central Road (CC) 1300 m, Left.
Distribution
From Honduras to Bolivia, Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in mainly very humid climates on both slopes, 10-1,300 m.
Habit
Tree, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion, short branches; glabrous twigs; stipules absent.
Bark
Reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion.
Leaves
Compound odd-pinnate leaves, alternate, leaflets 5-13, 7.5-23 x 2.5-11.2 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, apex short-acuminate, base asymmetric, opposite, glabrous or slightly pubescent on the underside near the central vein, margin entire; petiole 4-20 cm long.
Flowers
Flowers (unisexual) white to yellowish-green and cream; sepals 5, 0.4-0.9 mm long; petals 5, 1.4-2.2 mm long; stamens (8-) 10, unequal, staminodes present in pistillate flowers. The inflorescences have a broad subterminal panicle, with many flowers, 10-35 cm long, rusty-puberulent.
Fruits
Fruit a drupe, 1-1.8 x 0.8-1.3 cm, ovoid, oblong or obovoid, exocarp dark purple to black, endocarp cartilaginous.
Seeds
Seed 1.
Diagnosis
Characterized by its compound leaves, leaflets with entire margins, asymmetric at the base and secondary veins weakly forming a submarginal vein (brochidodromous venation), young leaves with silky pubescence on the underside. Its vegetative appearance and trunk color, as well as its inner bark, resemble or may confuse it with a species of Trichilia (Meliaceae), hence its vernacular names. In mature trees, when making a cut on the trunk, it secretes a slight milky sap in the cambium area.
Habitat
In the rainforest, both in primary forest and secondary vegetation.
Phenology
Flowers observed in May, fruits in October.

Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub 10. Maquira Aubl. By C.C. Berg. Trees or shrubs, dioecious. Leaves alternate, distichous on lateral branches; blade leathery, margins entire, pinnate-veined; stipules not completely amplexicaul, free. Inflorescences on spurs in the axils of the leaves, unisexual, discoid-capitate, involucrate. Staminate inflorescences often several together, pedunculate; flowers not covered by the inner involucral bracts before anthesis, numerous; perianth 4-parted to 4-divided; stamens 4; pistillode absent. Pistillate inflorescences subsessile; flowers numerous; perianth 4-lobed; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, tongue-shaped. Fruit-bearing perianth enlarged, fleshy, orange; fruits adnate to the perianth; seed large, without endosperm, cotyledons thick and equal. 4 spp. Tropical America.

Distribution
Nicaragua to southern Brazil, Bolivia, and Peru. In Costa Rica, widespread on both slopes, in humid to very humid climates, 0-1200m?. Common in LS.
Habit
Trees, 10-30 m tall.
Trunk
Straight or sometimes curved at the base, cylindrical, smooth outer bark; red sap; stipules absent.
Bark
Smooth outer bark; red sap.
Leaves
Simple, alternate leaves, 8–25 x 2.7–9 cm, oblong to narrowly oblong-ovate, apex acute to acuminate, base obtuse to truncate or subcordate, with a short pubescence of star-shaped trichomes and glaucous or whitish on the underside, secondary veins 10-28 per side, margin entire; petiole 0.8-2.5 cm long.
Flowers
Staminate inflorescences panicles with many flowers, tepals 3-4, 1.5–3 mm long; anthers 3(-4); pistillate flowers solitary or in clusters of 3-7 cm long; ovary 1-carpellate.
Fruits
Drupe fruit, 10-30 per inflorescence, 1.5–3 x 1-1.7 cm, subglobose to ellipsoid, dehiscent in 2 valves, densely reddish-starry.
Seeds
Subglobose seed, the aril lacerated.
Diagnosis
Recognized by its typical whorled branching, long horizontal branches, distichous leaves, with a truncated or rounded base, the blade with a whitish underside and a pubescence of short star-shaped hairs. Sometimes confused with
V. koschnyi,
but the trees of
V. sebifera
develop lesser height and diameter, the leaves generally have a truncated base, the secondary veins more distant from each other and not forming an evident submarginal vein near the margin, sometimes glaucous on the underside.

Tree, ca. 5-30(-40) m. Leaves imparipinnate, 10-30 cm; petiole and rachis generally canaliculate, glabrous or sparsely puberulent; leaflets 5-9, alternate (rarely subopposite), 10-15(-20) X 2.5-4.5 cm, narrowly elliptical or oblong to oblanceolate, attenuated at the base, acute to acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous, generally glabrous, with 13-16 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences axillary, thyrsoid, 10-20 cm, glabrous or puberulent. Flowers with petals white to yellowish-green. Fruits yellow to orange, 1.4-2 X 0.8-1.2 cm, oblong to ellipsoid, densely verrucous (with prominent warts often connected by irregular stripes), often sparsely adpressed-pubescent, with 3 or 4 valves; seeds 1 or 2, black, 0.8-2.2 cm, the aril red. Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the Parque Nacional Carara], [in the Puriscal region (in the Parque Nacional La Cangreja)], [in the Parque Nacional Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica and Panama], [in Ecuador and Peru], [in Northeast Brazil].

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Forest, Tree with plate # 926.
Distribution
From Nicaragua to Colombia and Venezuela. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid climates of the Caribbean slope and the central part to the southwest of the Pacific slope, 0-750 (-1000) m.
Habit
Tree or shrub, 3-10 m tall.
Leaves
Simple leaves, alternate, 3-17 × 1-6 cm, elliptical, elliptic-oblong or oblanceolate, long acuminate apex, attenuated base, glabrous, margin subentire, crenate or serrate.
Flowers
Yellowish or white-greenish flowers; sepals 4, very small; petals absent; stamens 1. Inflorescences racemose, solitary or 2-3 per axil, 4-14 cm long.
Fruits
Fruit capsule, 3-4 mm long, globose, orange when ripe.
Seeds
Seeds 1 (-3), smooth, with a red to orange aril.
Diagnosis
Characterized by its distichous leaves, with finely serrated margin, relatively thin blade, and fine scalariform tertiary venation. When in bloom, distinguished by its slender and pendulous inflorescence.
Habitat
In the Forest; Central Road (CC).
Phenology
Flowers and fruits observed at the end of August.

Adult plants frequent in the forest; seedlings common and recognizable by the large orbicular fimbriate stipules. Flowers in the late rainy season (August to November). The fruits mature within 1 month. Costa Rica to Peru and Brazil. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Colon and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone (Pipeline Road), Veraguas, and Panama (Cerro Jefe). [Paullinia turbacensis] is a tendriled liana; stems terete, ± glabrous, bearing conspicuous brown lenticels; sap at periphery milky, not copious. Leaves trifoliolate; petioles to 14 cm long, with marginal ribs above, glabrate; leaflets broadly elliptic, acuminate or acute at apex, attenuate to rounded at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-12 cm wide (to 23 cm long and 11 cm wide as juveniles), glabrate but with axillary tufts below, subentire to remotely crenate-dentate. Thyrses small, helicoid, to 7 cm long, solitary or clustered at nodes, often on leafless stems near the ground but occurring to 5 m high; flowers white, ca 5 mm long; petals with the scales ca two-thirds as long as petals, yellow-crested, the anterior scales bilobed, their appendages pubescent, the glands white, acute, densely pubescent; staminal cluster equaling petals; filaments densely pubescent; nectar abundant, stored near the large glands; ovary glabrous; styles pubescent. Capsules elliptic to obovate, 2 cm long, red, short-pubescent, the 3 boat-shaped valves broadly spreading to expose seeds; seeds 1-3, black, shiny, less than 1 cm long, covered on the lower half by a fleshy white aril, dangling on a thin funiculus when fully displayed.

Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the National Park Carara], [in the Puriscal region] (P.N. La Cangreja), [in the National Park Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica] and [in Panama], [in Ecuador] and [in Peru], [in Northern Brazil]. Trichilia tuberculata is distinguished by its densely verrucous fruits and restricted distribution in [Costa Rica] to very humid forest of the Pacific slope.

Ca. 52 genera and 2850 species, S Can.-Chile and Ven., Trin. & Tob., Guayanas, Bras., Par., Uru., Arg., Antilles, Bahamas, tropical and subtropical of the Old World; 18 genera and 146 species in Costa Rica. Shrubs or trees, rarely suffrutices or (Cassytha) parasitic herbs, hermaphroditic or (less frequently) polygamous, monoecious or dioecious, glabrous or (less frequently) pubescent, with sap generally watery, the foliage usually aromatic, sometimes nauseating (e.g., Cinnamomum sp. 1); stipules absent. Leaves simple, alternate and spiral or (less common) opposite or subopposite (Beilschmiedia, Caryodaphnopsis), entire, usually petiolate. Inflorescence axillary or pseudoterminal, paniculate or (less frequently) racemose, cymose or umbellate, rarely spicate, capitate or with 1 solitary flower. Flowers are bisexual or (sometimes) functionally unisexual, actinomorphic, white to yellowish or green, rarely pink or red, ± small, with a well-developed hypanthium (receptacle) (which looks like a calyx tube), usually persistent and accrescent in fruit, the pedicel sometimes thickened in fruit; members of the perianth (tepals) 6 (in Costa Rica), in 2 whorls of 3 each; stamens functional (3)6-9(12), with or without filament, generally arranged in 3(4) whorls, the 2 outer whorls (which usually appear as one) are absent (rarely) or composed of 6 separate stamens, very similar to each other, the middle whorl is composed of 3 separate stamens (often connivent or connate in Licaria), generally with 2 glands on both sides of each, the inner whorl is absent or composed of 3 staminodes; anthers dehiscent by (1)2-4 valves that open from the base to the apex, usually introrse in the outer whorls (apical-extrorse in Povedadaphne, lateral-extrorse in Pleurothyrium), usually extrorse in the middle whorl; pistil 1, simple; ovary superior (in Costa Rica), unilocular; ovule 1; placentation apical or subapical; style 1; stigma capitate or discoid. Fruit is berry-like or drupe-like, usually green or blackish and held until wrapped by the expanded hypanthium (cup), sometimes reddish, discoid to patelliform (like a plate or cup) or hemispheric to nearly globose, thin to fleshy or woody, smooth to warty or ribbed; seed 1, without endosperm.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.
